title: Anchor Elements
summary: Introduces HTML attributes through the anchor element: <a> only becomes a working hyperlink once it has an href attribute holding the destination URL. Covers attribute syntax, element-specific versus global attributes (draggable as the example), and an exercise that builds an ordered list of five favourite-website links, with a bonus step using the ol start attribute.

concepts.heading: What an attribute is and where it goes
points: An attribute adds extra information to an element, for example where a link should point.
Attributes always go inside the opening tag: after the tag name, before the closing angle bracket >. Never in the closing tag.
Syntax: tag name, a space, the attribute name, =, then the value in double quotes. Example: <a href="https://www.producthunt.com/">.
An element can have any number of attributes. Separate them with spaces, all inside the same opening tag: <a href="..." draggable="true">.
Why the quotes: the value is plain text (a string), and the quotes separate that text from HTML's own reserved words such as a, li or href. A URL is just text, so it is quoted.
VS Code autocompletion helps: start typing href inside the opening tag, pick it from the suggestions and press Enter. It inserts href="" and places the cursor between the quotes ready for the URL.

concepts.heading: The anchor element <a>
points: and wrap the clickable content of a hyperlink. The text between the tags is what the user sees and clicks.
Without an href attribute the element is not an active link: the text displays as ordinary text and nothing happens on click.
Add href="URL" and the browser immediately styles it as a link (blue and underlined by default) and clicking it navigates to that URL.

href is the anchor's key attribute. MDN's page for <a> lists all of its element-specific attributes; only a few are used in the course, and some listed there are deprecated and no longer used in HTML5.

(Extra) Other common anchor attributes: target="_blank" opens the link in a new tab; title="..." shows a tooltip on hover; download suggests saving the linked file. href can also be a relative path (another page of your own site, covered in the next section), #id (jump within the page) or mailto:address.

concepts.heading: Element-specific vs global attributes
points: Element-specific attributes only make sense on certain elements: href on <a>, start on <ol>, and so on.
Global attributes are available on every HTML element. MDN keeps a separate list of them.

Example used: draggable takes true or false and sets whether the element can be dragged. With draggable="true" on the anchor you can click and drag it around; without it, a drag attempt just selects the text.
Same syntax as any other attribute: name, =, quoted value, inside the opening tag.

(Extra) Global attributes you will meet constantly: id, class, style, title, lang, hidden. Note that links with an href and images are already draggable by default in most browsers, so draggable shows its effect most clearly on elements like p or div; real drag-and-drop behaviour also needs JavaScript.

concepts.heading: Nesting links in a list
points: For a list of links the structure is three layers deep: ol > li > a. The anchor sits inside the list item, which sits inside the ordered list.
The list numbers are not blue because they come from the ol/li, not from the anchor; only the anchor's content is styled as a link.
Reading MDN for an element (here <ol>) to find extra attributes is a skill the course wants you to practise.

concepts.heading: The ol start attribute (bonus challenge)
points: MDN's <ol> page lists a start attribute: an integer that sets the number the list counts from.
Put it in the opening ol tag: <ol start="5">. A five-item list then shows 5 to 9 instead of 1 to 5.
(Extra) Related ol attributes: reversed (counts down) and type (1, a, A, i, I).

concepts.heading: (Extra) Reference repo notes
points: The reference solution links to the repo author's own profiles (GitHub, portfolio, LinkedIn, Instagram); those personal links are replaced with neutral examples in the solution below, and the author footer is dropped.
It writes the list twice, once plain and once with start="5", to show both the main task and the bonus. One list is enough; add or remove start as needed.
Long anchors are wrapped over several lines by the formatter; that has no effect on the output.

concepts.heading: Study habit
points: After each lesson, jot down anything that was new to you; the course deliberately reuses earlier topics (lists, nesting) to reinforce them.

task.name: 3.3 Anchor Elements: my top 5 favourite websites
task.starting_point: index.html contains only the h1 'My Top 5 Favourite Websites'. goal.png shows an ordered list numbered 1-5 where each entry's text is a blue clickable link.
task.goal: Build an ordered list of five links to your own favourite websites, each opening the right site when clicked. Bonus: make the list count from 5 instead of 1.
steps: Inside each li add an and type the site's name between the tags as the link text.
In each opening a tag add href="..." with the full URL (including https://) of that site.
Open Live Preview and click each link to check it goes to the right place.
Bonus: look up <ol> on MDN, find the start attribute, and add start="5" to the opening ol tag so the list reads 5 to 9.
task.expected_result: A numbered list of five site names; the names are blue and underlined, the numbers are not, and every link navigates to its site. With the bonus, numbering runs 5-9.

solution_code.code:
My Top 5 Favourite Websites

  1. Product Hunt
  2. MDN Web Docs
  3. Wikipedia
  4. CodePen
  5. Stellarium

pitfalls: Leaving out href, so the text shows but is not a link.
Putting the attribute in the closing tag or outside the angle brackets.
Forgetting the quotes around the value, or mixing quote types (href="...').
Missing https:// so the browser treats the address as a relative path on your own site.
Putting the a outside the li (directly inside the ol) instead of inside it.
Putting start on an li or in the closing instead of the opening ol tag.

playground.coverage: Covers <a> with href, link text, an ordered list of five favourite sites (ol > li > a), target="_blank" as an extra, an explore demo that rebuilds the tag as href/text/target/title change (including emptying href), and notes on attribute syntax, kinds of href and meaningful link text.
gaps_and_ideas: Add the course's bonus task: use the ol start attribute so the list counts 5-9, with a pointer to MDN's <ol> attribute list.
Explain element-specific vs global attributes explicitly. Add a draggable="true" toggle to the explore demo (applied to a p, where the effect is visible) next to href.
Add a one-line note on why attribute values are quoted (they are text, distinct from reserved words like a, li, href).
Add a note that the list numbers stay black because they belong to the li, not the anchor.
target="_blank" is not in this lecture; label it as an extra and mention that modern browsers apply rel="noopener" to it automatically.
Add a 'spot the bug' task: an anchor with the href in the closing tag, one with missing quotes, and one missing https://.
